questions.q: What practical value does this lesson say a shared vocabulary of named integration patterns provides to architects?
options: It eliminates the need for any integration testing
It lets two architects quickly agree on roughly what's being proposed, instead of one describing a one-off mechanism that turns out to be an already well-understood pattern
It guarantees that every integration project finishes faster
It replaces the need for interface contracts between systems
questions.explain: Named patterns give architects a shorthand: saying 'this needs a Content-Based Router' communicates a well-understood design with known trade-offs immediately, rather than requiring a from-scratch description of a custom mechanism.

questions.q: A component inspects the actual content inside a message — such as an order's dollar amount — and routes it differently depending on what it finds. Which pattern is this?
options: Message Translator
Aggregator
Content-Based Router
A plain Message Router that routes only on message type
questions.explain: A Content-Based Router is specifically the pattern that inspects a message's actual content — not just its type or origin — to decide where it goes, such as routing high-value orders to manual approval based on an amount field.

questions.q: What does a Message Translator do, as distinct from a Message Router?
options: It decides where a message goes next without altering its content
It converts a message from one format or structure to another so two systems with different data shapes can exchange information
It collects multiple related messages into one consolidated message
It deletes a message once it has been successfully delivered
questions.explain: A Message Translator's job is format/structure conversion — reshaping a message so two systems with different data shapes can still exchange information — distinct from a Router's job of deciding destination without altering content.

questions.q: A batch job waits for every expected line-item feed file for an order to arrive before combining them into one complete order-status update. Which pattern is this job performing?
options: Content-Based Router
Message Translator
Aggregator
A plain point-to-point connection
questions.explain: An Aggregator collects multiple related messages and waits for a defined condition (all expected items arriving, or a time window elapsing) before combining them into a single consolidated message, rather than passing each piece along separately.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why does recognizing these named patterns matter specifically for an architect reviewing someone else's integration design?
options: It lets the architect identify, for example, that routing logic buried in an if/else chain is actually a Content-Based Router, and ask whether a more maintainable declarative tool would express the same intent
It is purely academic trivia with no practical review value
It only matters for integrations that use MuleSoft specifically
It replaces the need to understand the business requirements behind the integration
questions.explain: Recognizing the pattern underneath ad hoc code lets an architect evaluate whether a more maintainable, declarative implementation (a Flow decision element, an iPaaS router component) would express the same design intent more clearly — a concrete review skill, not just vocabulary.
